extracted.intended_audience: Catholic educators, university teachers, and students/scholars of English literature
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and reflective criteria about cultivating a Catholic literature within the English language and university context — what can and cannot be expected, how literature forms, and how universities should approach composition and style.

rubrics_metrics.name: Literature is a national and historical fact
rubrics_metrics.description: “A Literature, when it is formed, is a national and historical fact; it is a matter of the past and the present, and can be as little ignored as the present, as little undone as the past.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Literature cannot be prescribed or immediately remade by institutions; it reflects the history, character, institutions, customs, and collective life of a people. Any attempt to evaluate or produce literature must respect its rootedness in national history and circumstances.

rubrics_metrics.name: Classics are fixed and cannot be created at will
rubrics_metrics.description: “By the Literature of a Nation is meant its Classics... we cannot write a new Milton or a new Gibbon; we cannot expurgate what needs to be exorcised. They are great English authors...”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Universities should not aim to 'manufacture' canonical authors or expect immediate production of classics; the status of classics is the product of long historical recognition and cannot be conferred by programmatic effort alone.

rubrics_metrics.name: Formation of literature requires territory and a long period
rubrics_metrics.description: “If a literature be, as I have said, the voice of a particular nation, it requires a territory and a period, as large as that nation’s extent and history, to mature in.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: First-rate literary excellence is the outcome of an extended process (or rare accident). Curricula and institutional aims should be realistic about temporal and social limits on producing lasting literature.

rubrics_metrics.name: Authors are products of their age and circumstances
rubrics_metrics.description: “Each is, in his turn, the man of his age, the type of a generation, or the interpreter of a crisis. He is made for his day, and his day for him.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating or creating works, pay attention to how a writer’s subject-matter, tone, and form arise from contemporary events and social conditions (e.g., Hooker, Clarendon, Hobbes, Addison). Literary relevance often depends on this fit.

rubrics_metrics.name: Great authors help create and shape the language
rubrics_metrics.description: “Certain masters of composition... have been the making of the English language; and as that language is a fact, so is the literature a fact, by which it is formed... They have made it rich, harmonious, various, and precise.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Aiming for originality of style that enriches the language is a valid literary aim; influential writers' phrasing and diction often become vernacular and shape future expression. Teaching and practice can encourage contributions to language, not merely conformity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Style can be sui generis and remain influential apart from sense
rubrics_metrics.description: “How real a creation, how sui generis, is the style of Shakespeare, or of the Protestant Bible and Prayer Book... even were the subject-matter without meaning... the style would... remain as perfect and original a work as Euclid’s elements or a symphony of Beethoven.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate style as an independent achievement: distinctive stylistic mastery can have enduring cultural influence even when detached from particular content; encourage stylistic originality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Literary improvement spreads via schools and imitation
rubrics_metrics.description: “These gifted writers act upon the spoken and written language by means of the particular schools which form about them respectively... the literary schools... consist for the most part of mannerists, none of whom rise much above mediocrity; but they are... serviceable as channels... by means of which the achievements of genius may be incorporated into the language itself.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Imitation and the formation of stylistic schools are natural mechanisms for diffusing literary techniques; institutions can foster positive imitation while being aware of the risk of mannerism.

rubrics_metrics.name: The dominance of a classic may discourage innovation
rubrics_metrics.description: “The influence of a great classic upon the nation... on the other hand he discourages in some measure any advance beyond his own... The school which he forms would fain monopolize the language... and is intolerant of innovation.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Beware reverence for canonical writers that ossifies taste and blocks new directions; evaluators and teachers should balance respect for classics with encouragement of inventive departures.

rubrics_metrics.name: A matured language tends to become stereotyped; the age favors good writing over genius
rubrics_metrics.description: “It is not a day for great writers, but for good writing, and a great deal of it... While our literature in this day... is rich and various, its language is elaborated to a perfection far beyond that of our Classics... In point of mere style, I suppose, many an article in the Times... is superior to a preface of Dryden’s.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In less ‘formative’ literary periods, practical excellence, polish, and wide competence in style are achievable and valuable goals; educational programs should emphasize producing much competent, well-crafted writing appropriate to contemporary standards.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cultivate individuality and the personal voice
rubrics_metrics.description: “What they lack is that individuality, that earnestness, most personal yet most unconscious of self... The Epic was sung by the voice of the living, present poet... The ‘I’ of the Spectator... are the respective symbols of the two ages in our literature. Catholics must do as their neighbours; they must be content to serve their generation...”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Personal, identifiable voice (the ‘I’) lends persuasiveness and lasting interest; avoid anonymous, purely impersonal modes when the aim is to edify and move a contemporary audience.

rubrics_metrics.name: Universities should not try to reverse history but work with present literary forms
rubrics_metrics.description: “I have no dream of Catholic Classics as still reserved for the English language... I mean a literature which resembles the literature of the day... when I speak of the formation of a Catholic school of writers, I have respect principally to the matter of what is written, and to composition only so far forth as style is necessary to convey and to recommend the matter.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Institutional strategy: focus on producing Catholic writing that fits contemporary forms and style to convey Catholic truth effectively, rather than attempting to recreate past classical canons.

rubrics_metrics.name: Accept the moral imperfection and mixed nature of national literatures
rubrics_metrics.description: “National Literature is... the untutored movements of the reason, imagination, passions, and affections of the natural man... with all its richness and greatness, will necessarily offend the senses of those who... are exercised to discern between good and evil.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Critical engagement requires acknowledging that literature contains both excellence and moral failings; evaluation should balance appreciation of artistic merit with moral discernment rather than expecting doctrinal purity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Foreign influence can dilute a language’s nationality and idiom
rubrics_metrics.description: “When a language has been cultivated... there is another impediment... the effect which foreigners, or foreign literature, will exert upon it... The consequence will be, that the language in question will tend to lose its nationality—that is, its distinctive character...”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be mindful of excessive foreignizing tendencies; preserve idiomatic national character while allowing beneficial exchanges. In curriculum and composition, encourage national linguistic resources rather than wholesale adoption of foreign modes that may tame or corrupt the idiom.
